old:
Many essential Spanish verbs require specific prepositions that differ entirely from English equivalents:

• **con**: *soñar con* (to dream of/about), *contar con* (to count on / have at disposal)
• **en**: *pensar en* (to think about), *insistir en* (to insist on), *confiar en* (to trust in)
• **de**: *depender de* (to depend on), *enterarse de* (to find out about), *acordarse de* (to remember)
• **a**: *acostumbrarse a* (to get used to), *negarse a* (to refuse to).
new:
You know from B1 Unit 57 that many verbs go with a fixed preposition (*acostumbrarse a*, *darse cuenta de*). Here are more of the most useful ones; the preposition often differs from English:

• **con**: *soñar con* (to dream of/about), *contar con* (to count on / have at disposal)
• **en**: *pensar en* (to think about), *insistir en* (to insist on), *confiar en* (to trust in)
• **de**: *depender de* (to depend on), *enterarse de* (to find out about), *acordarse de* (to remember)
• **a**: *acostumbrarse a* (to get used to), *negarse a* (to refuse to).

old:
Spanish has two distinct ways to translate 'but':

• **Pero**: Adds a contrast, nuance, or limitation to a statement (positive or negative):
  *Estudié mucho, pero no aprobé.* (I studied a lot, but didn't pass.)
• **Sino**: Used strictly **after a negative clause** to substitute or correct an element (*not X, but rather Y*):
  *No quiero té, sino café.* (I don't want tea, but coffee.)
  *No es español, sino portugués.* (He is not Spanish, but Portuguese.)
• **Sino que**: Used when the correction contains a **conjugated verb**:
  *No fue al cine, sino que se quedó en casa estudiando.* (He didn't go to the movies, but rather stayed home studying.)
new:
You know *pero* ('but') from A1. New here: when the first part is negative and the second part corrects it, Spanish uses *sino* or *sino que*:

• **Pero**: Adds a contrast, nuance, or limitation to a statement (positive or negative):
  *Estudié mucho, pero no aprobé.* (I studied a lot, but didn't pass.)
• **Sino**: used **after a negative clause** to correct one element (*not X, but rather Y*):
  *No quiero té, sino café.* (I don't want tea, but coffee.)
  *No es español, sino portugués.* (He is not Spanish, but Portuguese.)
• **Sino que**: Used when the correction contains a **conjugated verb**:
  *No fue al cine, sino que se quedó en casa estudiando.* (He didn't go to the movies, but rather stayed home studying.)

old:
Spanish has no neuter nouns, but possesses the powerful neuter article **lo**. When combined with the masculine singular form of an adjective, it converts the adjective into an abstract noun meaning 'the [adjective] thing' or 'what is [adjective]':

• **lo bueno**: the good thing / what is good
• **lo malo**: the bad thing / the downside
• **lo importante**: the important thing / what matters
• **lo difícil**: the difficult part / what is hard
• **lo mejor / lo peor**: the best thing / the worst thing.
new:
You know *lo que* ('what') from B1 Unit 39. New here: **lo** before an adjective, in the masculine singular, means 'the [adjective] thing' or 'what is [adjective]':

• **lo bueno**: the good thing / what is good
• **lo malo**: the bad thing / the downside
• **lo importante**: the important thing / what matters
• **lo difícil**: the difficult part / what is hard
• **lo mejor / lo peor**: the best thing / the worst thing.

old:
When expressing intensity or degree, **lo + adjetivo / adverbio + que** translates to 'how [adjective/adverb] ... is/was!':

• **With adjective** (agrees in gender and number with the noun!):
  *No sabes lo difícil que fue el examen.* (You don't know how difficult the exam was.)
  *Mira lo contentas que están las chicas.* (Look how happy the girls are.)
• **With adverb** (invariable):
  *¡No te imaginas lo rápido que corre!* (You can't imagine how fast he runs!)
  *Me sorprende lo bien que hablas español.* (I'm amazed at how well you speak Spanish.)
new:
You met *lo* + adjective in the last lesson (*lo importante*). With *que* it also means 'how … it is / was!':

• **With adjective** (agrees in gender and number with the noun!):
  *No sabes lo difícil que fue el examen.* (You don't know how difficult the exam was.)
  *Mira lo contentas que están las chicas.* (Look how happy the girls are.)
• **With adverb** (invariable):
  *¡No te imaginas lo rápido que corre!* (You can't imagine how fast he runs!)
  *Me sorprende lo bien que hablas español.* (I'm amazed at how well you speak Spanish.)
